ety.text: Old Norse ǫfugrder. Middle English awke English awk Proto-Indo-European *wert-der. Proto-Germanic *wardaz Old English -weard English -ward English awkward From awk (“odd, clumsy”) + -ward. Compare Middle English aukeward (“in the wrong direction”).

senses.d: Lacking dexterity in the use of the hands, or of instruments.
ex: John was awkward at performing the trick. He'll have to practice to improve.

senses.d: Not easily managed or effected; embarrassing.
ex: That was an extremely awkward moment. Everyone was watching.

senses.d: Lacking social skills, or uncomfortable with social interaction.
ex: Things got awkward when my boss tried a cheesy pick-up line on me.
These cabinets are going to be very awkward when we move.

senses.d: Someone or something that is awkward.
ex: That is a way to make awkwards. And it's not fun to hang out with awkwards more than once.
